title: ENTERPRISE MULTI-AGENT AI ASSISTANT
description: Employee-facing financial assistant built on a supervisor with specialist sub-agents for accounts, loans, contributions, beneficiaries and enrollment, with RAG grounding, integrated guardrails, evals and prompt tracing across dev, staging and production.

caseStudy.overview: A chat assistant for a company's employees that answers questions and gets financial and benefits tasks done in one place. Behind a single chat window, a supervisor agent routes each request to a specialist sub-agent (self-directed account, loan, contribution, beneficiary, enrollment and more), grounded in the company's own documents and data. Every message passes through guardrails on the way in and on the way out, and every prompt is traced and evaluated across environments.
caseStudy.problem: Employees had to hunt through portals, PDFs and phone queues to answer questions about loans, contributions, beneficiaries or enrolling in a plan, and each topic lived in a different system. A single general-purpose chatbot was not an option: financial answers must be correct, grounded in the right policy, and safe, and a wrong or leaky answer has real consequences. The company also had an internal team that owned AI safety policy, so the assistant had to plug into their guardrails and not invent its own.
caseStudy.approach: I split the problem the way the business is split. A supervisor agent classifies intent and delegates to domain sub-agents, each with its own tools, knowledge and instructions, orchestrated with LangGraph and run on AWS Bedrock AgentCore. Retrieval keeps answers grounded in company content. Around the agents I integrated the internal team's guardrails web app on both input and output, then went beyond wiring it up: I built the evaluation sets, drove down false positives, and set up monitoring and tracing for prompts in dev, staging and production, so quality and safety could be measured and not assumed.

agentic.intro: The assistant is a team of agents, not one prompt. A supervisor understands the request and hands it to the specialist that owns that part of the business, then assembles one clear answer for the employee.

steps.title: Supervisor agent
steps.text: Classifies each message, keeps the conversation state, decides which specialist (or several) should act, and merges their results into a single reply. Ambiguous requests get a clarifying question instead of a guess.

steps.title: Specialist sub-agents
steps.text: Separate agents for self-directed accounts, loans, contributions, beneficiaries and enrollment, each with its own tools, data access and instructions, so each stays small, testable and easy to change without touching the others.

steps.title: LangGraph orchestration
steps.text: The flow is a LangGraph graph: nodes for routing, tool calls, retrieval and response, with explicit state and edges. That makes handoffs, retries and human-in-the-loop steps predictable and easy to trace.

steps.title: Bedrock AgentCore runtime
steps.text: Agents run on AWS Bedrock AgentCore, which handles hosting, identity and memory for the agents, so the team focused on behaviour rather than infrastructure.

steps.title: Grounded with RAG
steps.text: Policy documents and plan rules are ingested, chunked and embedded. Sub-agents retrieve the relevant passages and answer from them, with sources, to cut hallucinations on rules that must be exact.

steps.title: Tools with real actions
steps.text: Agents call internal APIs to read balances, start a request or update a record. Anything that changes data is explicit and confirmed with the employee first.

steps.title: Guardrails on the way in and out
steps.text: Each user message is checked before an agent sees it, and each answer is checked before the user sees it, using the internal team's guardrails service. Blocked content gets a safe, helpful fallback.

steps.title: Evals, tracing and monitoring
steps.text: Every prompt and response is traced across dev, staging and production. Evals score routing, retrieval, answers and guardrail decisions, and the scores are watched on dashboards, so a change to a prompt, model or tool shows up as a number before it reaches employees.

features: One chat for loans, contributions, beneficiaries, enrollment and self-directed accounts
Supervisor and specialist sub-agents, each with its own tools and knowledge
Retrieval grounded in company policy documents, with sources
Integrated internal guardrails on both input and output
Evals and scoring across routing, retrieval, answers and guardrails, using logic-based checks and LLM-as-judge
False-positive reduction so safe questions are not blocked
End-to-end tracing and monitoring of prompts in dev, staging and production
Confirm-before-act for anything that changes an employee's data

challenges.title: Guardrails that protect without blocking
challenges.text: Early on, legitimate questions about loans or beneficiaries were being flagged. I collected those cases into a labelled set, found the patterns behind each false positive, and worked with the guardrails owners and the prompts to fix them, re-running the full set after every change so fixes never reopened real risks.

challenges.title: Two kinds of checks, used where each fits
challenges.text: Some input and output checks are deterministic logic: pattern and rule checks that are fast, cheap and explainable, for things like sensitive identifiers. Others need judgement, so an LLM acts as judge with a written rubric for relevance, groundedness and policy. Choosing the right kind for each check kept cost and latency down without losing coverage.

challenges.title: Measuring quality, not guessing
challenges.text: The evals cover the whole pipeline, not just the final answer: routing (did the supervisor pick the right sub-agent), tool selection, retrieval, answer correctness and guardrail decisions on input and output. Each run is scored, with logic-based scores where an answer can be checked exactly and an LLM judge with a rubric where it needs judgement, and the scores are tracked per prompt version and per environment. A prompt or model change has to hold those scores before it moves from dev to staging to production.

challenges.title: Seeing inside a multi-agent run
challenges.text: A single question can touch a supervisor, two sub-agents, retrieval and several tools. Tracing every step with the same prompt versions in each environment made it possible to find which agent or prompt caused a bad answer, and to compare dev, staging and production behaviour.

challenges.title: Working across teams
challenges.text: The guardrails belong to another team. I integrated against their service and contract, fed back the false positives and gaps I found, and agreed how policy changes roll out, so the safety team and the product team could move without blocking each other.

architecture: Next.js chat UI streaming responses from the backend
Supervisor and sub-agents orchestrated as a LangGraph graph, hosted on AWS Bedrock AgentCore
Retrieval layer over a vector store for policy and plan documents
Guardrails service called before the agents (input) and before the reply (output)
Tracing and monitoring per prompt and per environment, with eval jobs scoring samples
Separate dev, staging and production configurations with promoted prompt versions
impact: One place for employees to ask about and act on their financial benefits
Answers grounded in company documents, with fewer hallucinations
Safety policy enforced consistently on every input and output
Fewer false-positive blocks, so the assistant stays useful
Prompt and model changes are measured before release, not after

title: CROSS-PLATFORM MOBILE APP
description: End to end cross platform mobile application (iOS & Android) with scalable architecture and optimized performance for smooth, high quality user experiences at scale.

caseStudy.overview: A production-grade cross-platform mobile application built with React Native, delivering smooth, high-quality user experiences on both iOS and Android from a single codebase.
caseStudy.problem: Maintaining separate native apps was costly and slow, while unoptimized React Native implementations suffered from janky interactions, excessive re-renders, and inconsistent behavior under high user activity.
caseStudy.approach: Designed a scalable architecture with efficient navigation and state-driven interfaces. Optimized rendering to reduce re-renders and ensure consistent, responsive behavior even under heavy concurrent usage.
features: Single codebase for iOS & Android
State-driven mobile interfaces
Efficient navigation and data handling
Performance optimization with reduced re-renders
Consistent behavior under high user activity

title: MICRO-FRONTEND ARCHITECTURE
description: Architected a micro-frontend setup using Module Federation, enabling independent deployments, reducing coupling, and significantly improving team productivity.

caseStudy.overview: A modular, scalable frontend architecture using Module Federation to split the platform into independently deployable micro-frontends, dramatically improving maintainability and team velocity.
caseStudy.problem: A monolithic frontend created bottlenecks: slow builds, tightly coupled code, and blockers where one team's changes stalled another. Scaling the team and adding features became increasingly risky and slow.
caseStudy.approach: Architected a micro-frontend setup using Webpack Module Federation. Each domain became an independently built, versioned, and deployed micro-app that shared consistent UI primitives through a federated shell.
features: Independent micro-frontend deployments
Shared component library via Module Federation
Decoupled domain ownership
Faster, isolated builds and releases
Improved maintainability and scalability
impact: Reduced development time for new features by 30%

title: AI CLINICAL SCRIBE — WEB PLATFORM
description: Web platform that listens to care visits and drafts the clinical note for review, backed by an agentic AI assistant that plans, calls tools across the clinic's data, and asks before it writes anything.

caseStudy.overview: A web platform for clinicians who visit patients and then have to write everything up by hand. It records the visit, transcribes who said what, drafts a structured clinical note, and hands it back to the clinician to review and approve. The same product also runs the day around the visit: patients, the appointment book, charting and an AI assistant. Behind it sits an agentic AI assistant that can look things up, build plans and take actions across the clinic's systems, with a person confirming anything that changes data.
caseStudy.problem: In the US, nurses and other clinicians often travel to patients' homes or see back-to-back appointments, and every visit ends with documentation. Notes get typed up between visits, after hours, or from memory. That is slow, tiring, and the first thing to go wrong when a day runs long: details are missed, charts fall behind, and clinicians burn out on admin instead of care. Generic dictation tools did not help much, because the output was a wall of text, not a note in the shape the chart needs.
caseStudy.approach: I treated the note as the product and the recording as the input. The visit is captured live, streamed for transcription with speaker turns, and turned into a structured note (summary, SOAP sections, action items and decisions) tied to the right patient and booking. The clinician is always the last step: they read the draft, fix it, and approve it before anything is exported or written back. Everything around it (today's visits, patient context, the appointment book) exists so the right patient is attached to a recording before it starts and the clinician rarely has to search for anything.
features: Consent-first recording flow with live transcript and speaker turns
Structured notes: summary, SOAP sections, action items and decisions
Today's visits view that attaches a recording to the right booking
Review and approval step before copy, export or write-back to the record
Audio playback synced to the transcript, with markers and comments
Sharing with access by role, PDF and transcript export
Appointment book with day, week and per-provider load views
Patient profiles with visit history, charts, photos and linked scribes
Agentic assistant with tool use, MCP, retrieval and confirm-before-write actions
AI assistant chat over WebSockets with a voice mode and file attachments
Feature flags and role-based access so each workspace sees only what it should

challenges.title: Recording that survives real conditions
challenges.text: Microphones get blocked, tabs lose focus, and networks drop mid-visit. The recording flow handles permission errors with plain explanations, pauses and resumes cleanly, keeps the audio when note generation fails, and offers a retry instead of losing the visit.

challenges.title: Long-running AI work in a fast UI
challenges.text: A note is not ready the moment recording stops. The list and note pages poll for processing, failed and write-back states, show the reason for a failure by error code, and let the clinician keep working while the note is generated.

challenges.title: Trust in a clinical setting
challenges.text: Nothing is final until a person approves it. Approval gates the exports, status rules decide what a clinician can do next, and multi-tenant headers and role checks keep each clinic's data separate.

challenges.title: A big product, kept safe to change
challenges.text: The app grew to many modules with several people shipping at once. An atomic component system, strict design tokens, lint and type checks on every push, and four test lanes (unit, mocked end-to-end, live-API, pre-push gate) kept changes reviewable.

architecture: Next.js 15 App Router with React 19 and TypeScript; server route handlers for auth, layout, support and proxying
Redux Toolkit and RTK Query for data, with contract tests against shared fixtures and schemas
WebSocket layer for chat and live transcription, kept opt-in so the text flow is never affected
Cookie-based session checks in middleware protect every dashboard route
Tailwind design tokens with Shadcn UI and dark/light themes; Biome and Lefthook enforce quality
impact: Turns a free-form conversation into a structured note the clinician only has to review
An assistant that does the lookup and planning work, such as finding patients to call for open slots, instead of only answering questions
Moves documentation out of evenings and into the visit itself
One product covers the visit, the schedule and the patient record, so context follows the clinician
Predictable releases through layered automated testing and CI gates

agentic.intro: The assistant is not a chatbot bolted onto the product. It is an agent: it reads the question, decides which tools it needs, calls them, looks at what came back, and repeats until it can answer, all streamed to the clinician as it works.

steps.title: Classify, then plan
steps.text: Each message is classified first (a patient lookup, a schedule question, a search, a request to act) so the model starts with the right tools and instructions instead of every tool at once.

steps.title: A multi-turn tool loop
steps.text: The model runs a reason, act, observe loop of up to 15 turns. It asks for a tool, gets the result, and decides the next step, so a question like "who could fill Thursday's open slot" becomes several dependent lookups ending in one short answer.

steps.title: One registry for every kind of tool
steps.text: Built-in functions, Lambda-backed data views and MCP servers all sit behind a single tool registry with the same contract: a definition, an executor and metadata. Adding a capability means registering a tool, not changing the agent.

steps.title: Parallel when safe, sequential when not
steps.text: An execution strategy detects dependencies between requested tools (pagination, a read that needs an earlier write) and runs independent calls in parallel, with per-source limits, and dependent ones in order.

steps.title: Built to fail gracefully
steps.text: Each tool has retries with exponential backoff, a circuit breaker and a fallback chain, so if the structured query fails the agent drops back to search instead of giving up. Failed calls come back to the model as data it can reason about.

steps.title: Grounded retrieval and memory
steps.text: Search fans out to the knowledge base, the database and conversation memory in parallel, then fuses, de-duplicates and reranks. Conversation summaries and patient context are stored per clinic, so answers stay consistent across sessions.

steps.title: Safe by construction
steps.text: Every tool call carries the clinic, user and patient context, and access is checked per request. Writes and sends need the user's confirmation. Content from uploaded files is treated as data, never instructions, which also guards against prompt injection.

steps.title: Rich results, not just text
steps.text: Tools return structured attachments (patient photos, documents, chart links, a live fill plan for open appointment slots) that the apps render as cards. The model only sees references, so no links or private data are made up or leaked.

steps.title: Observable and tested
steps.text: OpenTelemetry-style traces, metrics and token budgets cover every turn, and eval suites for routing and conversations catch regressions when prompts, tools or models change.

title: AI CLINICAL SCRIBE — MOBILE APP
description: The clinician's pocket version of the scribe: record a visit from the patient's home, see today's schedule and patient history, and review the note, all from a phone.

caseStudy.overview: A React Native app for clinicians who spend the day moving between patients. It carries the three things they need on the road: AI Scribe, the appointment book and the patient list. The web product was the source of truth, and I rebuilt its phone experience natively so a nurse in a driveway sees the same sections, wording, statuses and data they see at the desk.
caseStudy.problem: The people who most need to cut down on paperwork are the ones who are away from a desk. A home-care nurse cannot open a laptop in a patient's living room, so notes were written later, from memory, in the car or at night. The first mobile app was a thin shell: a flat list, a silent record button and plain-text summaries. It did not match the web, so clinicians had to learn two products, and it could not be trusted to behave the same.
caseStudy.approach: I rebuilt the app tab by tab against the web's phone view, using the web code as the specification: same sections in the same order, same colours and spacing, same status rules, same backend endpoints. Where the phone does something better natively (haptics, bottom sheets, share sheet, on-device speech), I used the native way and documented the difference. Each rebuilt area (Patients, Appointments, AI Scribe, More menu and settings) shipped with its own parity document, so reviewers and the next developer know what matches and what deliberately does not.
features: Bottom tab bar with AI Scribe, Appointments and Patients, plus a More menu
Recording flow with a consent dialog, speaker turns, floating dock and a visit-context sheet
Note page with Summary and Transcript tabs, SOAP note, action items, talk time and audio player
Approve, copy, export and share, with the web's messages and loading states
Appointment book with date strip, Mine/Everyone, week view and a booking-details sheet
Patient list with filters and pagination, and a full patient profile
Role-aware tab gating, including a scribe-only mode for clinicians who only need the scribe
Guided tour, in-app user guide, support reporting and settings
Times shown in the clinic's own time zone, not the phone's
White-label brand foundation: tokens, fonts, icons and native files

challenges.title: Parity without copy-paste
challenges.text: React on the web and React Native do not share components. I matched layout, copy and behaviour by reading the web source and rebuilding it with NativeWind, then recorded every intentional difference so parity stays a checkable claim, not a feeling.

challenges.title: Native speech and audio
challenges.text: Live speech recognition needs native modules, so it does not work in Expo Go. I built it on a development build, and made the app degrade safely: no crash when the native microphone module is missing, and clear errors when permission is denied or the mic stops.

challenges.title: Time zones and real-world data
challenges.text: Visits happen in the clinic's time zone, and some phones do not recognise every zone. I moved all schedule and recording times to the clinic's clock and added a guard so an unknown zone falls back instead of crashing.

challenges.title: Staying current on a fast-moving platform
challenges.text: I upgraded the app from Expo SDK 54 to 58 and React Native 0.88, replaced the removed audio library with the new one, and updated navigation, keeping the app building and shippable through EAS for both stores.

architecture: Expo SDK 58 and React Native 0.88 with React Navigation and TypeScript
Redux Toolkit slices plus RTK Query APIs for scribe, appointments, patients, approvals and chat
NativeWind for styling from the same design tokens as the web
expo-speech-recognition and expo-audio for capture and playback; expo-notifications for alerts
EAS Build profiles for development, beta and production, producing signed .aab and .ipa files
impact: Clinicians can start and finish documentation at the patient's side
One mental model across web and phone, so there is less to learn
Documented parity per screen makes reviews and future work faster
A current, store-ready build pipeline for iOS and Android
